name: kùláál, parler d'Iro
confidence_why: Pairault 1969, the only first-hand description of Kulaal (the Iro dialect of Boum Kabir), states that intensity carries no contrast and that two pitch heights do, an analysis that Boyeldieu, Kastenholz, Kleinewillinghöfer and Lionnet 2018 repeat, and Pairault's own later doubt (1981, 1994, 2001) concerns only whether every syllable bears tone or the language is better called pitch-accented, which the record already allows.
catalog_citation: Pairault, Claude. 1969. Documents du parler d'Iro, kùláál du Tchad. Paris: Librairie C. Klincksieck (Langues et littératures de l'Afrique noire, 5). 285 pp.
catalog_locator: Ch. 3 'Prosodie': §3-1 'Note liminaire' p. 49; §3-3 pp. 50-51 with n. 3 (p. 50); §3-4 'Deux hauteurs pertinentes' p. 51. Page anchors from Google Books search-within-volume (p.50 'accent syllabique de hauteur', p.51 '3-4 Deux hauteurs pertinentes', p.52 'tons ponctuels') and Boyeldieu et al. 2018:12 ('Pairault 1969: 49-54'); p.49 for §3-1 inferred (chapter start).
catalog_quote: [p.49] 3-1 Note liminaire. Dans le parler pòŋààl, l'intensité d'articulation est dénuée de valeur significative. [...] Un autre type d'opposition existe dans la langue de Boum Kabir: il s'agit de la hauteur mélodique, apte à différencier deux unités phonématiquement identiques. [...] [p.50] l'hypothèse du pòŋààl comme langue à accent syllabique de hauteur, accent marqué de façon mélodique par une opposition haut: bas. Dans cette perspective, un seul noyau syllabique était considéré comme support d'une hauteur distinctive dans le cadre du monème. En fait, pareille hypothèse multipliait les problèmes qu'elle tentait de résoudre. Ainsi: a) en présence de mots à syllabes isotones, comment identifier un accent de hauteur (3) ? [...] Au bout du compte, les données toléraient mieux l'analyse du [p.51] pòŋààl comme langue à tons, c'est-à-dire une langue dans laquelle chaque syllabe est dotée de hauteur (relative) déterminée. Dans cette langue, la syllabe se définit elle-même comme unité tonale. [n. 3, p.50] Ou tout au moins un accent syllabique dans chaque mot ? Cette formulation de la question laisse intacte (et inexplorée) l'hypothèse d'un traitement prosodique du pòŋààl par l'« accent de mot » [...] 3-4 Deux hauteurs pertinentes. [...] deux hauteurs seulement interviennent de manière significative: ce sont les deux « tons » dits haut et bas.

new_statements.translation: 3-1 Preliminary note. In the pòŋààl dialect, articulatory intensity has no distinctive value. [...] Another type of opposition exists in the language of Boum Kabir: melodic pitch, able to differentiate two phonemically identical units. [...] [p.50] the hypothesis of pòŋààl as a language with a syllabic pitch accent [...] In fact, such a hypothesis multiplied the problems it tried to solve. [...] In the end, the data were better accommodated by the analysis of pòŋààl as a tone language, i.e. a language in which every syllable carries a determined (relative) pitch. [...] only two pitch levels are significant: the two 'tones' called high and low.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kulaal (reference dialect pòŋààl of Boum Kabir) is analysed as a two-tone language (H, L; every syllable tone-bearing, contour tones on long vowels); intensity (dynamic stress) is explicitly stated to be non-distinctive, and an earlier one-pitch accent-per-word analysis (Pairault 1966: 423) is explicitly rejected. No positional word-stress rule is given.
new_statements.exceptions: None as to stress. Extra (3rd/4th) pitch registers attributed to expressive intonation or register shift ('décalage de registration') at clause/sentence boundaries. Footnote 3 (p.50) explicitly leaves 'intact and unexplored' a possible word-accent treatment (à la Rowlands on Mandinka); Pairault later (Cahiers du LUTO 1981; 1994: 29 n.14; 2001) doubted that every syllable bears significant pitch and suggested Kulaal might rather be a 'langue à accents de hauteur' with two heights and two lengths — never worked out, and no linguist has since re-examined Kulaal prosody (Boyeldieu et al. 2018: 12).
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns the word/moneme in the pòŋààl dialect (Boum Kabir), Pairault's reference variety; based on texts and lexicon, impressionistic (no instrumental data). Access caveat: the 1969 text was read only through chained Google Books full-text snippets (book has no preview); page numbers from Google's search-within-volume hits and from Boyeldieu et al. 2018's citation 'Pairault 1969: 49-54'. Verification against the printed pages is desirable.
new_statements.identity_note: All statements concern the pòŋààl dialect of Kulaal spoken at Boum Kabir (Boum-le-Grand), Pairault's reference variety; Pairault 1969:11 distinguishes four varieties (páṭóól, pòŋààl, tɩ́ààlà, tííṭààl), all under gula1265 [glj]. Do not confuse with 'Kulaale' [kʊ̀láːlɛ̀], a Fania/Fanya variety (fani1244) documented by Lionnet (LDD 17, 2020), nor with Bon Gula/Zan Gula ('Goula du Guéra').

Quand Pascal Boyeldieu ira-t-il passer quelques mois sur place pour résoudre le [problème ...]
new_statements.translation: 14. I am now convinced that my 'tonology' of Kulaal would need to be revised from top to bottom: this language does, I think, have two significant pitch heights, but it does not seem to me at all certain that it is for all that a 'tone language', that is, a language in which every syllable carries a significant pitch height. When will Pascal Boyeldieu go and spend a few months on the spot to solve the [problem ...]

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's existing statement from Pairault 1969 ch. 3 (intensity of articulation has no significative value; two pertinent pitch heights, 'deux tons dits haut et bas'): the two significant heights are reaffirmed and no stress is claimed. It adds the author's later doubt (1994) that all syllables carry pertinent pitch, which weakens the 'full tone language' label toward a pitch accent-like system; it does not touch stress placement. two attempts used.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No stress rule. The note is about tone only: Pairault retracts confidence in his 1969 two-tone analysis, still holds that Kulaal has two significant pitch heights, but doubts that every syllable bears a pertinent height, i.e. doubts that it is a tone language in the strict sense (leaving open a restricted-tone / pitch accent type analysis). Nothing on intensity stress, prominence or its position.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources concern the parler d'Iro (pòŋààl / Boum Kabir village, Lake Iro, Chad), the same variety as the catalog's Pairault 1969 record; no other dialect is described.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on stress: neither source claims word stress. Pairault 1969 (already in the catalog) says intensity has no significative value and that two pitch heights (tones H/L) are pertinent on every syllable; Pairault 1994 n. 14 keeps the two significant heights but withdraws confidence that every syllable carries a pertinent height, so the tonal TYPE (full two-tone language vs. restricted tone / pitch accent) is left open by the author himself; the 1981 LUTO interview snippet already held by the project says the same ('langue à accents de hauteur' floated, then 'j'ai opté pour une langue à deux tons'). Boyeldieu et al. 2018 (§4.4, held by the project) still describe Kulaal as having 'only two tones'. This is a tone-vs-pitch accent hedge, not a stress conflict.
